946.title: Tashlich, casting away
946.hook: Jews cast crumbs into flowing water, symbolizing sins cast away (Micah 7:19)
946.howItsDone: On the afternoon of Rosh Hashanah, some Jews go to a river, stream or sea to recite verses from Micah and the Psalms; some toss bread crumbs onto the water, and some shake out their pockets.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Yamim Noraim, the ten days from the new year to the Day of Atonement. Your line was ten days.

An afternoon by a river. People in the kind of clothes you'd wear to synagogue stand along the bank, some holding small prayer books. A grandfather lifts a child so she can see over the rail. Someone tosses a few crumbs of bread onto the water, and the current carries them downstream. A woman turns her coat pockets inside out and shakes them over the edge. Nobody is feeding the ducks, exactly. They're acting out a line from one of the prophets, about where wrongs go.
screen: `AN AFTERNOON BY A RIVER.` → `CRUMBS ON THE CURRENT.` → `A LINE FROM A PROPHET.`

segments.voice: First, the verse. The prophet Micah ends his book with a question and a promise. In the King James words: "Who is a God like unto thee, that pardoneth iniquity, and passeth by the transgression of the remnant of his heritage? he retaineth not his anger for ever, because he delighteth in mercy." And then: "He will turn again, he will have compassion upon us; he will subdue our iniquities; and thou wilt cast all their sins into the depths of the sea." Second, the name. In Micah's Hebrew, the word for thou wilt cast gives the custom its name: tashlich. On Rosh Hashanah, in the afternoon, Jews in some places walk to flowing water, a river, a stream, the sea, and say verses from Micah and the Psalms. Some toss crumbs; some shake out their pockets. Third, what the crumbs are. The bread doesn't carry the sins away by itself. In the tradition's own telling, the turning back, the teshuvah, is the work. The crumbs are a picture of it, something for the hands to do: you watch the thing go where you can't reach it anymore. Fourth, the end of a stretch. Tashlich closes the Jewish voices on forgiveness: the return, four steps, ask them first, Joseph weeping, Esau running, ten days, and now the river. Notice who does the casting in Micah's verse. Not the person. God casts the sins into the depths, and the depths, in the verse's picture, are a place nobody goes to fish them back out.
screen: `HE DELIGHTETH IN MERCY.` · `THOU WILT CAST: TASHLICH.` · `THE CRUMBS ARE A PICTURE.` · `INTO THE DEPTHS OF THE SEA.` · then, large: `CAST IT AWAY.`

segments.voice: If there's water near you, even a bowl on the table, bring a leaf or a small scrap close; if not, picture one. Give it one thing you're ready to put down, a resentment, a regret, an old wrong you've already turned from, then let it drop onto the water, or let it go in your mind, and watch it drift without reaching for it. If you pray, you can say a line from Micah.
Tashlich. Hebrew, from Micah's thou wilt cast: the custom on Rosh Hashanah of going to flowing water and casting crumbs, a picture of wrongs cast away. Today's word.
Your line: cast it away. Into the depths, where nobody fishes. That's day nine hundred forty-six.

947.title: As we forgive
947.hook: forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors (Matthew 6:12)
947.howItsDone: Christians pray the Lord's Prayer in private and together in church; depending on the church and the translation, the line says debts, sins or trespasses.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Tashlich: crumbs on moving water, sins cast into the depths. Your line was cast it away. Today, the Christian voices begin.

A stadium before a game. A hospital chapel at night. A classroom, a wedding, a funeral. Somewhere right now, people are saying the Lord's Prayer together, some fast and some slow, a few half a beat behind. And in the middle comes a line people say so smoothly they sail right past it. Forgive us, as we forgive. Two words sit in that line like a hinge: as we. The person praying asks for mercy, and in the same breath ties that mercy to their own.
screen: `SAID IN STADIUMS AND CHAPELS.` → `A LINE THAT GOES BY FAST.` → `TWO WORDS LIKE A HINGE.`

segments.voice: Start with the words Jesus taught, in Matthew's Gospel. The King James has it: "And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors." Debts. The picture is a ledger: somebody owes, and forgiving means letting the bill go unpaid. Second, the other versions. Luke's Gospel gives the prayer a little differently: "forgive us our sins; for we also forgive every one that is indebted to us." And the Book of Common Prayer, the Church of England's prayer book, says trespasses: "forgive us our trespasses, As we forgive them that trespass against us." Debts, sins, trespasses. Churches still say it different ways, and each word lights a different corner of the same room. Third, the hinge. Right after the prayer, Matthew has Jesus come back to one line: "For if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you." Of all the prayer's lines, this is the one the text stops to underline. Christians read it more than one way. Some hear a condition: mercy received and mercy given come as a pair. Others hear a description: a heart that has really taken in forgiveness starts to give it away, the way a full cup spills. Christian teachers have argued over that balance, and the prayer holds it without settling it. Fourth, the plain fact of saying it. Each time someone prays this line, they name their own debts and their debtors in one sentence. For anyone, praying or not, that's a mirror: what am I asking to be let off, and what am I still holding over someone else?

segments.voice: Bring to mind one modest debt someone owes you, a borrowed book, an apology that never came, a favor not returned, and see their name on one line of a ledger. Picture tearing up that line, not because it didn't matter, but because you choose to stop collecting, and notice what happens in your chest. If you pray, you can say the line from the Lord's Prayer slowly, with that person in mind.

948.title: Seventy times seven
948.hook: Peter asks: seven times? Jesus: seventy times seven (Matthew 18:21–22)
948.carry: a number too big to keep track of
948.howItsDone: Christian teachers turn to Matthew 18:21–22 when speaking about forgiveness in families and congregations, and preachers sometimes pair it with the verses just before it on going to the person who wronged you.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was trespasses, and the hinge in the Lord's Prayer: as we forgive. Your line was a full cup spills.

How many times is enough? Ask it about the roommate who leaves the dishes, again, or the coworker who takes credit in the meeting, says sorry after, and does it the next week. The first time, letting it go feels generous. The third time it feels foolish. Somewhere around there, a reasonable person starts asking where the line is. Peter, one of Jesus's closest followers, asked exactly that, out loud, and even offered a number that sounds generous. Today: seventy times seven.
screen: `AGAIN. AND AGAIN.` → `WHERE'S THE LINE?` → `PETER OFFERS A NUMBER.`

segments.voice: First, the question. Matthew tells it in two short verses. In the King James words, Peter asks: "Lord, how oft shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? till seven times?" Not a stranger: my brother, someone close, who will keep showing up. And Peter's number isn't stingy. Seven times is a lot of patience with one person. Second, the answer. Jesus says: "I say not unto thee, Until seven times: but, Until seventy times seven." Some readers take the Greek as seventy times seven, others as seventy-seven times. Either way, it isn't a bigger number to count up to. It's a number too big to keep track of. The answer quietly takes the counting away. Third, a companion line. Luke's Gospel has a version that is even more domestic: "if he trespass against thee seven times in a day, and seven times in a day turn again to thee, saying, I repent; thou shalt forgive him." Seven times in one day. Not a betrayal once a decade: ordinary life, with someone you live alongside. Fourth, what it doesn't say. It doesn't tell Peter to pretend nothing happened. In Matthew, the verses just before lay out how to go to a brother who has wronged you and speak to him directly. Some Christian teachers read the two together: you can name the wrong, set a limit, even keep your distance, and still refuse to keep a running total in your heart. Forgiveness, in this reading, is about the count kept inside, not about letting harm continue.

segments.voice: Picture one thing someone close to you does again and again, nothing dangerous, just something that wears on you, and notice the little counter in your head: the fifth time, the tenth. Set the counter down; you can still think it's wrong and still plan to talk about it, and each time the tally comes back, breathe out and set it down again. If you pray, you can name that person once more, without a number attached.
Peter. The disciple who asked Jesus how often to forgive, and got an answer too big to keep count. Today's word.

949.title: The unforgiving servant
949.hook: a man forgiven a huge debt throttles someone over a small one (Matthew 18:23–35)
949.howItsDone: Christians read the parable of the unforgiving servant as part of Jesus's answer to Peter about forgiveness, since Matthew places it right after seventy times seven.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Peter, who asked how often to forgive. Your line was a number too big to keep track of.

A king sits down to go through his accounts, and one servant is brought in owing him ten thousand talents. The text says plainly he has nothing to pay it with. The king orders him sold, with his wife and children and everything he has. The servant falls down before him and begs: be patient, I'll pay it all. And the king, moved with compassion, lets him go and forgives the whole debt. The servant walks out a free man. What he does next is the whole story.
screen: `TEN THOUSAND TALENTS.` → `BE PATIENT, I'LL PAY IT ALL.` → `THE WHOLE DEBT, FORGIVEN.`

segments.voice: First, the turn. Outside, the forgiven servant runs into a fellow servant who owes him an hundred pence, in the King James words. A small sum beside an impossible one. He "laid hands on him, and took him by the throat, saying, Pay me that thou owest." The fellow servant falls down and begs with almost the same words: "Have patience with me, and I will pay thee all." The same plea that just saved the first man. He refuses, and has him thrown in prison until he pays. Second, the witnesses. The other servants see it, are very sorry, and tell the king everything. Mercy, and the lack of it, gets noticed. Third, the question at the center. The king calls the man back and asks: "Shouldest not thou also have had compassion on thy fellowservant, even as I had pity on thee?" That's the whole parable in one line. His problem isn't that he wanted his money. He walked out of the biggest mercy of his life and let it change nothing about how he treated anyone else. Fourth, the hard ending. The king hands him over to the tormentors, and Jesus closes with a warning about forgiving a brother from the heart. Christians read that ending differently. Some take it as a stark warning about judgment. Others hear a picture of what an unforgiving heart already does to itself: it locks itself in. Both readings keep the same center. The man forgot he had been forgiven.
screen: `BY THE THROAT, OVER A SMALL DEBT.` · `THE OTHER SERVANTS SEE IT.` · `EVEN AS I HAD PITY ON THEE.` · `A HARD ENDING, READ TWO WAYS.` · then, large: `SHOULDEST NOT THOU ALSO HAVE HAD COMPASSION?`

segments.voice: Remember a time someone let you off: a parent who didn't stay angry, a friend who took you back, a stranger who was kind when you'd been rude. Stay with what they chose not to collect, then let someone come to mind who owes you something small, and hold the two side by side, the way the story does. If you pray, you can give thanks in your own tradition's words for the mercy you received.
Talents. The enormous debt, ten thousand of them, that a king forgave a servant who then seized a fellow servant over a small one. Today's word.
Your line: I was forgiven too. The king's question still stands. That's day nine hundred forty-nine.

950.title: Father, forgive them
950.hook: from the cross: they know not what they do (Luke 23:34)
950.howItsDone: Christians remember this line among the sayings of Jesus from the cross, read especially on Good Friday, and some churches meditate on the sayings one by one that day.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was talents: the huge debt forgiven, and the small one seized. Your line was I was forgiven too.

Luke's Gospel slows down at the place called Calvary. Two criminals, one on each side. A crowd standing and watching. And before the soldiers cast lots for his clothes and the mocking that follows, Luke records a sentence from Jesus. It isn't a cry of pain. It isn't a curse. It's addressed upward, and it's about the people right in front of him. Today: Father, forgive them.
screen: `A PLACE CALLED CALVARY.` → `TWO CRIMINALS, ONE ON EACH SIDE.` → `A SENTENCE ADDRESSED UPWARD.`

segments.voice: First, the line itself. In the King James: "Then said Jesus, Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do." Notice the first word. Father. The same word that opens the prayer Jesus teaches in Luke, said here, of all places. Not judge, not avenger. The family word, spoken from the worst day. Second, who he forgives. The sentence names no names, and Christians have read it in different ways. Some hear it about the soldiers carrying out orders. Some widen it to everyone who had a hand in it. Others widen it further still, to every person, themselves included. The text leaves the circle open, and that openness is part of its force. Third, the reason he gives. For they know not what they do. Some readers point out that they know what their hands are doing; what they don't see, in this reading, is what it means: who this is, what it costs, what they've become part of. Read that way, the line holds two truths at once. A wrong is happening. And the people doing it don't fully understand it. Forgiveness here doesn't pretend the first truth away. It leans on the second. Fourth, ordinary life. Sometimes the people who hurt us aren't villains with a plan. They're tired, scared, careless, following orders, repeating what was done to them. They know what they did. They may not see all of what it did. In that gap, between the act and the understanding, this sentence plants itself. It doesn't make the wrong smaller. It makes room for the person.
screen: `FATHER: THE FIRST WORD.` · `THE CIRCLE LEFT OPEN.` · `THEY KNOW WHAT, NOT WHAT IT MEANS.` · `ROOM FOR THE PERSON.` · then, large: `FOR THEY KNOW NOT WHAT THEY DO.`

segments.voice: Let one person who wronged you come into view, not to relive it, just enough to see their face, and ask quietly what they didn't understand: what it would cost you, what was happening in them, something they still can't see. You don't have to excuse them; simply wish them one thing, that someday they see it clearly. If you pray, you can bring them into your prayer with the line from Luke.
Father. The first word of Jesus's prayer from the cross in Luke, forgiving the people who didn't know what they were doing. Today's word.
Your line: they know not. Even there, the first word was Father. Day nine hundred fifty.

951.title: Neither do I condemn thee
951.hook: a woman is brought for stoning, and the crowd leaves one by one (John 8:1–11)
951.howItsDone: Christians read the story of the woman taken in adultery from John 8 as a picture of mercy joined to a call to change.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Father, the first word of a prayer from the cross. Your line was they know not.

What should happen to her? That's the question put to Jesus early one morning in the temple, where he's sitting and teaching. Some scribes and Pharisees, John's Gospel says, bring a woman and set her in the middle. Caught in adultery, they say, in the very act. The law of Moses says such a person should be stoned. What do you say? The text is plain that it's a trap: any answer can be used against him. Everyone is watching. The woman stands there alone. And Jesus doesn't answer. He bends down and writes on the ground with his finger.
screen: `A WOMAN IN THE MIDDLE.` → `A QUESTION THAT'S A TRAP.` → `HE WRITES ON THE GROUND.`

segments.voice: First, the silence. They keep pressing him, and he keeps writing. John never tells us what he wrote; people have guessed, and the text doesn't say. What it shows is a man refusing to be rushed into a verdict. Second, the sentence. Finally he stands and says, in the King James words: "He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her." Then he bends down and writes again. He doesn't argue the law or defend her. He turns the question from her to them, and looks down again, as if to give them room. Third, the leaving. Those who heard it, "being convicted by their own conscience, went out one by one, beginning at the eldest, even unto the last." The eldest first. Maybe the ones with the longest memories of their own mistakes. One by one, until only two people are left. Fourth, the last words. Jesus looks up and asks: "Woman, where are those thine accusers? hath no man condemned thee?" She says, "No man, Lord." And he says: "Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more." Both halves matter. He doesn't pretend nothing happened; he tells her to go and live differently. But he will not throw the stone, and he sends her out with a future instead of a sentence. Some Christians hear it as mercy that is neither cheap nor cruel. The scene ends on a question worth carrying: which stone am I still holding?
screen: `HE WRITES, AND WAITS.` · `WITHOUT SIN? CAST THE FIRST STONE.` · `ONE BY ONE, THE ELDEST FIRST.` · `NO CONDEMNING, AND A FUTURE.` · then, large: `NEITHER DO I CONDEMN THEE.`

segments.voice: Find one verdict you've already passed on someone, a relative, a coworker, someone in the news, maybe yourself, and feel its weight like a stone in your palm. Ask the story's question gently, with no blame: am I without anything like this myself? Then imagine your fingers loosening and the stone dropping; you can still think something was wrong, you're only putting down the throwing, and if you pray, you can pray for that person by name.
Accusers. The ones who walked away one by one, until none were left to condemn the woman caught in adultery. Today's word.
Your line: put down the stone. A future instead of a sentence. Day nine hundred fifty-one, done.

952.title: Zacchaeus gives back
952.hook: a hated tax collector is welcomed, and gives back fourfold (Luke 19:1–10)
952.howItsDone: Christians read the story of Zacchaeus as a picture of welcome leading to repentance and restitution.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was accusers, who walked away one by one. Your line was put down the stone. Today, forgiveness from the other side: the one who did the wrong.

Jericho, and the streets are packed because Jesus is passing through. Somewhere at the back of the crowd is a rich man who can't see a thing. Luke gives us his name, Zacchaeus, his job, chief among the tax collectors, and one more detail: he was little of stature. So he runs ahead and climbs a sycamore tree to watch from the branches. Jesus reaches the spot, stops, looks up, and calls him by name.
screen: `A CROWD TOO TALL TO SEE OVER.` → `A RICH MAN UP A TREE.` → `CALLED BY NAME.`

segments.voice: First, the invitation. In the King James words, Jesus says: "Zacchaeus, make haste, and come down; for to day I must abide at thy house." Not a lecture. Jesus invites himself to the man's house, and Zacchaeus comes down fast and receives him joyfully. Second, the grumbling. When people saw it, Luke says, they all murmured that he had gone to be a guest with a man that is a sinner. The welcome comes first, before any change, and the crowd doesn't like it. Third, the turn. Zacchaeus stands up and says: "Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold." Fourfold. Not an apology alone, not just what he took. Four times over. Nobody demands this of him in the story. It pours out of him once he's been welcomed. Fourth, the answer. Jesus says: "This day is salvation come to this house," and adds, "the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost." Some readers notice the order: the welcome came before the repair, and the repair was real and costly. Forgiveness, in this story, doesn't cancel making it right. It sets it free. And that closes the week: Tashlich, trespasses, Peter's question, the servant who forgot his forgiven talents, Father, forgive them, and a crowd putting down its stones. Zacchaeus adds the last piece: the one who has been welcomed gives back more than he took.
screen: `COME DOWN: TODAY, AT THY HOUSE.` · `THE CROWD MURMURS.` · `HALF TO THE POOR, FOURFOLD BACK.` · `WELCOME FIRST, THEN REPAIR.` · then, large: `I RESTORE HIM FOURFOLD.`

segments.voice: Turn the story around and find one old wrong you did, small enough to name and old enough that it's been quietly sitting there: a loan never repaid, a credit you took, a friend you dropped. Look at it squarely, without punishing yourself, and ask what giving it back would look like, a little more than even, until one concrete step comes to mind. If you pray, you can hold that step in your prayer.
Zacchaeus. The tax collector Jesus welcomed to dinner, who then promised half his goods to the poor and fourfold to anyone he had cheated. Today's word.
Your line: fourfold. The welcome came first, and the repair was real. See you tomorrow.
